units.title: Which Pair
units.blurb: A rate is always one currency against another.

units.title: What the Central Bank Is Doing
units.blurb: Hikes, cuts, hawks, doves, forward guidance.

units.title: Two Hands of Policy
units.blurb: Monetary and fiscal policy can pull apart.

units.title: Where the Money Runs
units.blurb: Risk appetite, safe havens, carry, intervention.

concepts.caption: The money a country or region circulates.
concepts.definition: The means of payment issued and enforced by a government.
concepts.example: The rupiah fell to a three-month low as Asian currencies struggled.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Currency is the money itself; the exchange rate is the ratio between two of them.

concepts.caption: How much of one currency buys another.
concepts.definition: The rate at which one currency converts into another.
concepts.example: The euro was down 0.21% at $1.1191 against the dollar.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The exchange rate is the ratio; currency is the thing being exchanged.

concepts.caption: The currency most trade and borrowing is denominated in.
concepts.definition: The US currency, and the unit most commodities and cross-border debt are priced in.
concepts.example: The dollar index rose 0.25% to 101.82.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The dollar is the US currency and the global funding currency; the euro is the shared currency of the euro area.

concepts.caption: One currency shared by many countries.
concepts.definition: The shared currency of the euro area, with policy set by the European Central Bank.
concepts.example: The euro declined and was headed for a weekly loss against the dollar.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The euro is the euro area's; the dollar is the US's. They form the most-traded pair.

concepts.caption: Japan's currency, long the funding currency of choice.
concepts.definition: The Japanese currency, often borrowed because of persistently low rates.
concepts.example: The yen was set for a weekly gain against the dollar.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Yen is Japanese; yuan is Chinese. They even share the ¥ symbol, so read the code (JPY vs CNY).

concepts.caption: China's currency — same symbol as the yen, different money.
concepts.definition: The unit of China's renminbi, international code CNY.
concepts.example: The yuan hit its highest level since 2022 on a weaker dollar.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Yuan is Chinese; yen is Japanese. Both use ¥, so only context or the code separates them.

concepts.caption: Britain's currency, also called the pound.
concepts.definition: The British currency, code GBP, also called pound sterling.
concepts.example: Sterling rose against the dollar and the euro after inflation data.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Sterling is Britain's; peso is the name several Latin American and Asian countries use.

concepts.caption: A currency name several countries share — check which one.
concepts.definition: The currency of Mexico, the Philippines, Argentina and others, each with its own code.
concepts.example: The rupiah and the peso weakened as the dollar firmed.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Peso is used by several countries (MXN/PHP/ARS); the rupiah belongs only to Indonesia.

concepts.caption: Indonesia's currency.
concepts.definition: The Indonesian currency, code IDR.
concepts.example: Indonesia's central bank intervened to slow the rupiah's slide.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The rupiah is Indonesia's alone; peso is a shared name.

concepts.caption: Your money buys more foreign currency than before.
concepts.definition: A rise in one currency's value against another.
concepts.example: The yuan appreciated to its highest level since 2022.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Appreciate means more valuable; depreciate means cheaper.

concepts.caption: Your money buys less foreign currency than before.
concepts.definition: A fall in one currency's value against another.
concepts.example: The Taiwan dollar depreciated against the US dollar.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Depreciate means cheaper; appreciate means more valuable.

concepts.caption: News shorthand for a currency getting more valuable.
concepts.definition: A plain-language term for a currency's value rising, used interchangeably with appreciate.
concepts.example: The yen strengthened as risk appetite faded.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Strengthen goes up; weaken goes down. Both are plainer than appreciate and depreciate, and more common in copy.

concepts.caption: News shorthand for a currency getting less valuable.
concepts.definition: A plain-language term for a currency's value falling, used interchangeably with depreciate.
concepts.example: Asian currencies weakened as the dollar firmed.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Weaken goes down; strengthen goes up.

concepts.caption: The institution that sets money supply and rates.
concepts.definition: The authority responsible for monetary policy, money supply and interest rates.
concepts.example: Investors awaited minutes from the central bank's latest meeting.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The central bank is the institution; monetary policy is what it does.

concepts.caption: The central bank pushes rates up.
concepts.definition: A central bank increase in the policy interest rate.
concepts.example: Traders reduced bets on a December rate hike.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A hike moves rates up; a cut moves them down.

concepts.caption: The central bank pulls rates down.
concepts.definition: A central bank reduction in the policy interest rate.
concepts.example: Markets priced a small chance of a rate cut before March.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A cut moves rates down; a hike moves them up.

concepts.caption: Leaning toward tighter policy, more worried about inflation.
concepts.definition: A monetary policy stance that favours tightening and prioritises fighting inflation.
concepts.example: A hawkish surprise strengthens a currency.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Hawkish leans tight and lifts the currency; dovish leans loose and weighs on it.

concepts.caption: Leaning toward looser policy, more worried about growth.
concepts.definition: A monetary policy stance that favours easing and prioritises supporting growth.
concepts.example: A dovish surprise weakens a currency.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Dovish leans loose and usually weakens the currency; hawkish leans tight.

concepts.caption: The central bank saying in advance what it intends to do.
concepts.definition: Communication about the future policy path, used to steer market expectations.
concepts.example: Forward guidance from each central bank matters more than the decisions themselves.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Forward guidance is talk about what will happen; tapering is actually buying less.

concepts.caption: The central bank gradually buys fewer bonds.
concepts.definition: Gradually scaling back asset purchases — the first step in exiting quantitative easing.
concepts.example: The Bank of Japan has been tapering its bond purchases.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Tapering reduces the addition (buying less); tightening is the actual squeeze. Tapering is not the same as tightening right away.

concepts.caption: The central bank steering the price and quantity of money.
concepts.definition: Policy that influences the economy through interest rates, money supply and credit conditions.
concepts.example: Monetary policy is now diverging across the major economies.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Monetary policy is the central bank's lever on money; fiscal policy is the government's lever on tax and spending.

concepts.caption: The government steering tax and spending.
concepts.definition: Policy that influences the economy through taxation and public spending.
concepts.example: France's fiscal policy is now working against monetary policy.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Fiscal is decided by government and parliament; monetary by the central bank. They can pull in opposite directions.

concepts.caption: The central bank buys assets at scale to flood the system with money.
concepts.definition: An unconventional policy of large-scale asset purchases to inject liquidity.
concepts.example: Quantitative easing pushed yield-seeking capital into emerging markets.
concepts.mixUpWhy: QE injects liquidity; tightening withdraws it.

concepts.caption: Anything that makes money dearer or scarcer.
concepts.definition: A policy stance that reduces money supply or raises funding costs, including hikes and smaller asset purchases.
concepts.example: A further reduction would tighten global liquidity.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Tightening squeezes; easing loosens.

concepts.caption: Anything that makes money cheaper or more plentiful.
concepts.definition: A policy stance that expands money supply or lowers funding costs, including cuts and asset purchases.
concepts.example: The market expects easing next year if growth slows.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Easing loosens; tightening squeezes.

concepts.caption: The same money buys less than it used to.
concepts.definition: A sustained rise in the general price level, eroding purchasing power.
concepts.example: Annual core consumer inflation exceeded the central bank's 2% target.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Inflation is prices rising; deflation is prices falling.

concepts.caption: Prices keep falling — which sounds good and is not.
concepts.definition: A sustained fall in the general price level, usually with weak demand and heavier debt burdens.
concepts.example: Some economists warned of deflation as goods prices fell.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Deflation is prices falling, which makes debt heavier in real terms; inflation is prices rising.

concepts.caption: No growth and still rising prices — the worst combination.
concepts.definition: The coexistence of stagnant growth and high inflation.
concepts.example: Economists debated whether the world is heading for stagflation.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Stagflation is stalled growth with high inflation; a soft landing is inflation cooling without a recession. Opposite outcomes.

concepts.caption: Inflation comes down without a recession.
concepts.definition: Inflation returning to target while the economy avoids recession.
concepts.example: A soft landing remains the central case, but the probability has narrowed.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A soft landing keeps growth while inflation falls; stagflation loses growth while inflation stays.

concepts.caption: Goods, services and income added up across borders.
concepts.definition: A country's net balance on goods, services and transfers — broadly, how much it relies on outside money.
concepts.example: Countries running a current account deficit depend on capital inflows.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The current account is the wider measure (goods, services, income); the trade balance counts goods only.

concepts.caption: Exports minus imports, goods only.
concepts.definition: The difference between a country's goods exports and imports — a component of the current account.
concepts.example: A trade balance that swings into deficit adds to the pressure.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The trade balance counts goods only; the current account adds services, investment income and transfers.

concepts.caption: The central bank steps into the market and buys its own currency.
concepts.definition: A central bank buying or selling its own currency to influence the exchange rate.
concepts.example: Indonesia's central bank intervened to slow the rupiah's slide.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Intervention is direct buying and selling of currency; tightening is a policy stance on rates and liquidity. Intervention can leave rates untouched.

concepts.caption: Money crossing borders, in and out.
concepts.definition: Investor money moving across borders — direct investment, portfolio investment and other flows.
concepts.example: Emerging markets depend on capital inflows to fund a current account deficit.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Capital flows are the financing side (money moving); the current account is the real side (trade and income). They mirror each other.

concepts.caption: Whether investors are willing to take risk.
concepts.definition: Investors' willingness to bear risk: when it is high money chases higher-yielding assets, when it is low it retreats to havens.
concepts.example: The yen strengthened as risk appetite faded.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Risk appetite is the willingness (can be high or low); risk-off is one specific state where it has collapsed.

concepts.caption: The market is scared and money is running for safety.
concepts.definition: A market state where investors withdraw from risk assets and move into havens.
concepts.example: The yen traded at firmer levels, encouraged by more risk-off conditions.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Risk-off is the market state (everyone leaving); a safe haven is where the money goes.

concepts.caption: What people buy when they are scared.
concepts.definition: An asset treated as a store of value in turmoil — the yen, the franc, gold, Treasuries.
concepts.example: The yen was supported by safe-haven demand after the selloff.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A safe haven is the asset being bought; risk-off is the state that causes the buying.

concepts.caption: Borrow where money is cheap, invest where it pays more.
concepts.definition: Borrowing in a low-yielding currency to invest in a higher-yielding one, earning the differential.
concepts.example: The carry trade has become less attractive as rate differentials narrow.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A carry trade is a market participant's strategy; intervention is a central bank's operation.
